methods.label: Compare two right triangles
methods.explanation:
The tangent suggests drawing the radius to \(D\), which creates a right triangle we can compare with the one at \(C\). Let \(O\) be the circle's center and let \(\alpha=\angle CAB\), where \(0<\alpha<90^\circ\).

Since \(OC\) lies on \(BC\), we have \(OC\perp CF\). Also, \(OD\perp DF\), because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact. Thus right triangles \(OCF\) and \(ODF\) have the common hypotenuse \(OF\) and equal legs \(OC=OD\). They are congruent by hypotenuse-leg congruence, so
\[
CF=DF.
\]
Because \(BC\) is a diameter, \(\angle BDC=90^\circ\). The points \(B,D,A\) are collinear, so \(\angle CDA=90^\circ\) as well. In right triangle \(BCD\),
\[
\angle CBD=90^\circ-\alpha,
\qquad \angle BCD=\alpha.
\]
This proves statement D. Since \(BC\perp CA\), it also gives \(\angle FCD=90^\circ-\alpha\).

The equality \(CF=DF\) makes triangle \(CFD\) isosceles, so \(\angle CDF=90^\circ-\alpha\). Subtracting this from \(\angle CDA=90^\circ\) gives \(\angle FDA=\alpha\). Now triangle \(AFD\) has equal angles at \(A\) and \(D\), hence \(FA=FD\), proving C. Together with \(CF=DF\), this gives \(CF=FA\), so \(F\) is the midpoint of \(CA\), proving A. Finally, the exterior-angle theorem in triangle \(AFD\) gives
\[
\angle CFD=\angle FAD+\angle FDA=2\alpha,
\]
proving E.

The two parts of \(\angle CDA\) are \(90^\circ-\alpha\) and \(\alpha\). They are equal only when \(\alpha=45^\circ\). For example, a right triangle with \(\angle A=30^\circ\) gives parts of \(60^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\). Thus statement B does not follow, and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

methods.label: Construct the midpoint of CA
methods.explanation:
The diameter gives a right angle at \(D\), so the midpoint of \(CA\) is useful. We will show that this midpoint must be \(F\).

Let \(O\) be the circle's center, let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(CA\), and write \(\alpha=\angle CAB\), with \(0<\alpha<90^\circ\). Since \(BC\) is a diameter, \(\angle BDC=90^\circ\). Because \(B,D,A\) are collinear, \(\angle CDA=90^\circ\). Thus \(CA\) is the hypotenuse of right triangle \(CDA\). Its midpoint is equally distant from the three vertices, giving
\[
MC=MD=MA.
\]
Triangles \(OCM\) and \(ODM\) have \(OC=OD\), \(CM=DM\), and the common side \(OM\), so they are congruent by SSS. Since \(\angle OCM=90^\circ\), we obtain \(\angle ODM=90^\circ\). The given tangent \(DF\) is also perpendicular to \(OD\). There is only one perpendicular to \(OD\) through \(D\), so \(DM\) and \(DF\) are the same line. Their intersection with \(CA\) is therefore \(M=F\).

Consequently,
\[
CF=FA=FD,
\]
which proves A and C. Triangle \(AFD\) is isosceles, so \(\angle FDA=\angle FAD=\alpha\). Its exterior angle at \(F\) is \(\angle CFD=2\alpha\), proving E.

Also, \(\angle CBD=\angle ABC=90^\circ-\alpha\). Right triangle \(BCD\) then gives \(\angle BCD=\alpha\), proving D.

At \(D\), the right angle \(CDA\) is divided into \(\angle FDA=\alpha\) and \(\angle CDF=90^\circ-\alpha\). These are equal precisely when \(\alpha=45^\circ\). Taking \(\alpha=30^\circ\), for instance, disproves the claimed bisection. Hence the statement that cannot be proved in general is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
